**1. System _1_ – Commutativity violation**

The addition operator is defined by  

\[
c+\tau = \det(\tau)\;c\odot\tau^{-1},
\]

where \(\odot\) denotes element‑wise (Hadamard) multiplication.  
For the two arbitrary square matrices \(m\) and \(a\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
X &= m + a = \det(a)\;m\odot a^{-1},\\[2mm]
Y &= a + m = \det(m)\;a\odot m^{-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Because \(\det(a)\) and \(\det(m)\) are generally different and the inverses \(a^{-1}\) and \(m^{-1}\) do not commute, \(X\neq Y\) in general.  

The multiplication operator is  

\[
v * x = \exp(v) + x^{\top}.
\]

Thus the forward‑order product is  

\[
\text{Result}=X*Y = \exp\!\bigl(\det(a)\;m\odot a^{-1}\bigr) + \bigl(\det(m)\;a\odot m^{-1}\bigr)^{\!\top},
\]

whereas the reverse‑order product would be  

\[
Y*X = \exp\!\bigl(\det(m)\;a\odot m^{-1}\bigr) + \bigl(\det(a)\;m\odot a^{-1}\bigr)^{\!\top}.
\]

Since, in general,  

\[
\exp\!\bigl(\det(a)m\odot a^{-1}\bigr) + (\det(m)a\odot m^{-1})^{\!\top}
\neq
\exp\!\bigl(\det(m)a\odot m^{-1}\bigr) + (\det(a)m\odot a^{-1})^{\!\top},
\]

the system is **not commutative**. The “commutativity‑violation measure’’ can be taken as the difference  

\[
\boxed{X*Y - Y*X = \exp\!\bigl(\det(a)m\odot a^{-1}\bigr) - \exp\!\bigl(\det(m)a\odot m^{-1}\bigr) + \bigl(\det(m)a\odot m^{-1} - \det(a)m\odot a^{-1}\bigr)^{\!\top}}.
\]

---

**2. System _2_ – Identity element**

Addition is  

\[
n + B = n(-x)\,B(x^{3}),
\]

so for an unknown element \(E_i\) we require  

\[
t + E_i = t \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t(-x)\,E_i(x^{3}) = t.
\]

Solving for \(E_i\),

\[
E_i(x^{3}) = \frac{t(x)}{t(-x)}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
\boxed{E_i(x)=\frac{t\!\bigl(x^{1/3}\bigr)}{t\!\bigl(-x^{1/3}\bigr)} }.
\]

The expression for \(E_i\) depends on the particular polynomial \(t\).  
If we replace \(t\) by the different polynomial \(\rho\) we obtain  

\[
E_i^{(\rho)}(x)=\frac{\rho\!\bigl(x^{1/3}\bigr)}{\rho\!\bigl(-x^{1/3}\bigr)},
\]

which, in general, is **not equal** to the former \(E_i(x)\). Hence the “identity’’ derived above is not universal; System _2_ has **no single element that works for all \(t\)**.

---

**3. System _3_ – Distributivity of “\(*\)” over “\(+\)”**

Addition: \(F+B = F(-x)+B(-x)\).

Multiplication: \(b*H = b(x\cdot4)-H(-x)\).

Take the three polynomials \(\xi, a, h\).

*Left‑hand side*  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\xi * (a+h) 
&= \xi\bigl(x\cdot4\bigr) - (a+h)(-x)\\
&= \xi(4x) - \bigl[a(-(-x)) + h(-(-x))\bigr]\\
&= \xi(4x) - \bigl[a(x)+h(x)\bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

*Right‑hand side*  

\[
\begin{aligned}
(\xi*a)+(\xi*h) 
&= \bigl[\xi(4x)-a(-x)\bigr] + \bigl[\xi(4x)-h(-x)\bigr] \quad\text{(using addition)}\\
&= \bigl[\xi(4x)-a(-x)\bigr](-x) + \bigl[\xi(4x)-h(-x)\bigr](-x)\\
&= \bigl[\xi(-4x)-a(x)\bigr] + \bigl[\xi(-4x)-h(x)\bigr]\\
&= 2\,\xi(-4x) - \bigl[a(x)+h(x)\bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{\xi * (a+h)=\xi(4x)-[a(x)+h(x)],\qquad
(\xi*a)+(\xi*h)=2\,\xi(-4x)-[a(x)+h(x)] }.
\]

Unless the special condition \(\xi(4x)=2\,\xi(-4x)\) holds (which is not true for generic polynomials), the two sides differ. Therefore **multiplication does not distribute over addition** in System _3_.

---

**4. System _4_ – Identity element**

Addition is defined by  

\[
\beta+e = \beta^{-1} - \operatorname{tr}(e)\,I.
\]

We seek \(E_i\) such that \(f+E_i = f\):

\[
f^{-1} - \operatorname{tr}(E_i)\,I = f
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\operatorname{tr}(E_i)\,I = f^{-1} - f.
\]

The right‑hand side is a matrix, while the left‑hand side is a scalar multiple of the identity. Equality can hold **only when \(f^{-1}-f\) itself is a scalar matrix**, i.e. when \(f\) is a \(1\times1\) matrix (a scalar).  

* For a general \(n\times n\) matrix the equation has no solution; thus System _4_ lacks a universal identity element.  

* In the trivial \(1\times1\) case we can solve explicitly:  

\[
\operatorname{tr}(E_i)=f^{-1}-f \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
\boxed{E_i = f^{-1}-f }.
\]

If we now replace \(f\) by another matrix \(v\), the same \(E_i\) would give  

\[
v+E_i = v^{-1} - \operatorname{tr}(E_i) = v^{-1} - (f^{-1}-f),
\]

which equals \(v\) **only when** \(v^{-1} - (f^{-1}-f)=v\), a condition that does not hold in general. Hence the element derived for \(f\) does **not work for \(v\)**.

Consequently, System _4_ has **no universal identity** (except in the degenerate \(1\times1\) case, where the identity depends on the specific matrix used).  

---  

**Summary**

1. System _1_: addition is non‑commutative; the forward‑reverse difference is  
\(\exp(\det(a)m\odot a^{-1})-\exp(\det(m)a\odot m^{-1})+(\det(m)a\odot m^{-1})^{\!\top}-(\det(a)m\odot a^{-1})^{\!\top}\neq0\) in general.  

2. System _2_: the “identity’’ would have to be \(E_i(x)=\dfrac{t(x^{1/3})}{t(-x^{1/3})}\), which depends on \(t\) and therefore fails for \(\rho\); no universal identity exists.  

3. System _3_: \(\xi*(a+h)=\xi(4x)-[a(x)+h(x)]\) while \((\xi*a)+(\xi*h)=2\xi(-4x)-[a(x)+h(x)]\); since the two expressions are not equal in general, distributivity fails.  

4. System _4_: the equation \(f+E_i=f\) forces \(\operatorname{tr}(E_i)I=f^{-1}-f\), which is impossible for non‑scalar matrices; only in the 1×1 case does \(E_i=f^{-1}-f\) work, but it does not work for a different matrix \(v\). Hence System _4_ has no universal identity.

The addition operation in System 13 is defined by  

\[
\sigma + C=\sigma^{T}\,C .
\]

To find an element \(E_i\) such that \(g+E_i=g\) we solve  

\[
g^{T}\,E_i=g .
\]

If \(g\) is invertible then  

\[
E_i=(g^{T})^{-1}g .
\]

*Verification:*  

\[
g+E_i=g^{T}\bigl((g^{T})^{-1}g\bigr)=\bigl(g^{T}(g^{T})^{-1}\bigr)g=I\,g=g .
\]

If we replace \(g\) by a different matrix \(y\) (with no relation to \(g\)), the required identity would be  

\[
E_y=(y^{T})^{-1}y,
\]

which in general is **not** equal to \((g^{T})^{-1}g\). Consequently  

\[
y+E_i=y^{T}E_i=y^{T}(g^{T})^{-1}g\neq y
\]

unless \(y=g\) (or \(y\) happens to be symmetric and satisfy the same condition). Hence the element \(E_i=(g^{T})^{-1}g\) works only for the specific matrix \(g\) and does not serve as a universal identity.

**14. Answer:**  
The multiplication in System 14 is  

\[
q*y=\det(y)\;q\;\odot y,
\]

where \(\odot\) denotes element‑wise (Hadamard) product.  

Take arbitrary \(2\times2\) matrices  

\[

I=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad 
\psi=\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{pmatrix}.
\]

*Left‑hand side*  

\[
Y*I=\det(I)\,Y\odot I=Y\odot I=
\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\0&d\end{pmatrix}=A.
\]

\[
A*\psi=\det(\psi)\,A\odot\psi=
\det(\psi)\begin{pmatrix}ap&0\\0&ds\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}ap\det\psi&0\\0&ds\det\psi\end{pmatrix}.
\]

*Right‑hand side*  

\[
I*\psi=\det(\psi)\,I\odot\psi=
\det(\psi)\begin{pmatrix}p&0\\0&s\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}p\det\psi&0\\0&s\det\psi\end{pmatrix}=B.
\]

\[
Y*B=\det(B)\,Y\odot B.
\]

Since \(B\) is diagonal, \(\det(B)=\det(\psi)^{2}ps\). Thus  

\[
Y*B=
\det(B)\begin{pmatrix}a\,p\det\psi&0\\0&d\,s\det\psi\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}a\,\det\psi^{3}p^{2}s&0\\0&d\,\det\psi^{3}ps^{2}\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Clearly  

\[
(Y*I)*\psi=
\begin{pmatrix}ap\det\psi&0\\0&ds\det\psi\end{pmatrix}
\neq
Y*(I*\psi)=
\begin{pmatrix}a\,\det\psi^{3}p^{2}s&0\\0&d\,\det\psi^{3}ps^{2}\end{pmatrix}
\]

in general (they coincide only for very special choices of \(\psi\)). Hence the multiplication operator “\(*\)” is **not associative** in System 14; i.e. \((Y*I)*\psi\neq Y*(I*\psi)\) for typical matrices.
